html:
From about 2400 BCE, square stamp seals in the style of the Indus Valley turn up in Mesopotamia, at cities such as Ur. They are physical proof of trade between the two oldest urban worlds. Sumerian and Akkadian texts call a distant land of trade Meluhha, and most scholars think it was the Indus Valley.

The texts say Meluhha sent carnelian, ivory, fine wood, gold and lapis lazuli. Sargon of Akkad boasted that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun docked at his capital. One Mesopotamian seal belonged to a man called the interpreter of Meluhha, so Indus traders, or people who spoke their language, lived there. Etched carnelian beads made in the Indus style lie in the royal graves of Ur.

Goods probably moved by sea along the coasts of the Gulf, through ports such as Lothal and Dilmun in Bahrain. Mesopotamian goods are rarer in Indus cities, and the Indus script on the seals is still unread. The trade faded after about 1900 BCE as the Indus cities declined; see Meluhha trade with Sumer.
